analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 43.3% of firms in professional, scientific, and technical services (NAICS 54, which includes legal) reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 41.9% in the prior period. The survey does not break legal out separately, so this is the broadest official adoption measure available for the sector.

What firms deploy is documented in some detail. Per Legaltech Hub, generative AI is taking over document review, first drafts, and due diligence. Steno's Transcript Genius mines deposition and trial transcripts for summaries, data points, and strategic insights. MiAI Law, an Australian platform, combines case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document and pleading verification. Per ILTA, Epiq announced Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access, while Litify expanded ACE with firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity. ILTA also describes a Discovery tool that reads the tools a firm already uses, finds repeated work, ranks it by the hours it costs, and turns any finding into automation.

Vendor activity is concentrating at the top of the market. Per Legaltech Hub, OpenAI released Astra for Law, built initially for Am Law 200 firms, described not as a new model but as a configuration pairing GPT-6 Astra with specific knowledge, tools, and ecosystem plugins tailored for legal use. Legaltech Hub positions itself as a directory where buyers research, vendors showcase, and investors understand the marketplace. The World of AI's Legal Models section tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads, and release date refreshed daily.

On returns, the sources report capability and deployment more than measured ROI. ILTA's Discovery tool ranks repeated work by the hours it costs, implying time savings as the metric. Legaltech Hub flags a problem efficiency metrics do not capture: some of the automated work, document review, first drafts, due diligence, was how junior lawyers learned judgment through repetition and supervision, and firms are experimenting with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those learning opportunities before the consequences emerge.

On risk and regulation, the ABA's Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence focused on six issues: AI and the Profession, AI Risk Management, AI and Access to Justice, AI Governance, AI Challenges ,  Generative AI, and AI and Legal Education. The task force has concluded its work, and the ABA Center for Innovation continues to address ethical considerations, provide guidance on the trustworthy and responsible development and use of AI, and identify strategies to mitigate AI-related risks. Past ABA webinars cover practical uses, key developments, and the ethical, professional responsibility, and regulatory considerations lawyers must navigate.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the picture is one of maturing infrastructure with active professional guardrails. Stanford CodeX, a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science, runs an accelerated program for agentic AI applications at the intersection of technology and law, a hackathon, and FutureLaw 2026, all aimed at computational law and legal AI. Vals AI provides private, domain-specific benchmarks in legal, tax, and finance, and lists Legal Research among routine knowledge work benchmarks. ILTA's observation that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs, combined with the ABA's guidance and the catalogues of tools and models, suggests the tooling is in place, but the profession's own bodies frame deployment around risk management, ethics, and the training of the next generation of lawyers.

https://www.iltanet.org/.brief: ILTA describes itself as a global resource community for legal technologists and notes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of large language models, with this spring’s Peer to Peer topics reflecting that evolution. Epiq announced the availability of Model Context Protocol connectors for its Epiq AI, Discover, Narrate, and Access products. Litify expanded its ACE offering with firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity. The page also states that Discovery reads the tools a firm already uses, identifies repeated work, ranks it by hours cost, and turns any finding into automation.

https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/.brief: Legaltech Hub presents itself as a worldwide catalogue of legal technology products and services, aimed at buyers, vendors, and investors. The page notes that OpenAI has released Astra for Law, a configuration of its GPT-6 Astra model tailored for legal work and initially built for Am Law 200 firms. It also highlights Steno’s Transcript Genius, an AI tool for analyzing deposition and trial transcripts, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, summarization, contract review, and document verification. A further item examines how generative AI automating document review and first drafts may remove learning opportunities for junior lawyers, and describes firm experiments with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those opportunities.

https://law.stanford.edu/codex-the-stanf.brief: CodeX is a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science that studies how information technology can improve legal processes. It applies data science and artificial intelligence to build quantitative and predictive models of the law, moving beyond traditional empirical analysis. The program offers a hands-on accelerated track for interdisciplinary student teams to prototype Agentic AI and the CFAA applications at the intersection of technology and law. CodeX also hosts a hackathon that brings together AI innovators, machine learning specialists, and legal professionals to prototype future legal technology. Additionally, it organizes an international conference and FutureLaw 2026 to bring together leaders in law, technology, and policy to discuss sustainable, ethical, and responsible AI in legal systems.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page reports that it lists the 1,000 most-downloaded open legal models on Hugging Face Hub, showing licence, download counts, and release dates, refreshed daily. It also lists books by Stephen R. Jordan, including “The Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. Additionally, the page catalogs several AI audit and assessment tools such as the AI Business Enablement Audit™, AI Readiness & Performance Assessment™, AI Risk & Governance Review™, AI Efficiency & Process Optimization™, AI IT Security Audit™, AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy™, Secure by Design in the Age of AI™, Application Security in the Age of AI™, and The AI Lawyer.

https://www.americanbar.org/groups/cente.brief: The Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has finished its work, and the Center for Innovation will keep addressing how AI affects the legal profession, including ethical issues, trustworthy development, and risk-mitigation strategies. It will also provide guidance on responsible AI use. Past webinars from the Task Force examine how AI is reshaping law practice, covering practical applications, new legal technology, and the ethical, professional-responsibility, and regulatory challenges lawyers must navigate.
